evals.prompt: We have three product lines that feel disconnected from each other. Should we put them all under one brand name or keep them separate?
evals.expected_output: Should frame this explicitly as a house-of-brands vs. branded-house vs. hybrid decision, not just a naming question. Should ask about the actual reason the lines feel disconnected (different audiences? different price points? different positioning?) before recommending a structure, since the right architecture depends on that. Should note the tradeoffs: branded house compounds marketing investment into one name but risks brand dilution if lines target very different segments; house of brands protects each line's positioning but multiplies marketing spend.
assertions: Frames the question as a brand-architecture decision (house of brands vs. branded house vs. hybrid)
Asks why the lines feel disconnected before recommending a structure
Explains the branded-house tradeoff (compounding investment vs. dilution risk)
Explains the house-of-brands tradeoff (protected positioning vs. multiplied spend)

evals.prompt: how do we even know if our brand is healthy? feels like a fuzzy question but the CEO wants a number
evals.expected_output: Should acknowledge the CEO's instinct is reasonable even if 'brand health' resists a single number. Should propose a small set of trackable proxies (aided/unaided awareness, consideration, NPS or a loyalty-adjacent metric, share of voice) rather than inventing one composite score. Should caution against treating any single metric as definitive, and note that brand health tracking needs a consistent cadence to be meaningful (one-off measurement is close to useless).
assertions: Proposes a small set of concrete trackable metrics rather than one invented composite score
Mentions awareness (aided/unaided) as a component
Cautions against over-indexing on any single metric
Notes the need for consistent measurement cadence, not a one-off snapshot

evals.prompt: We just had a product recall go badly on social media. How do we handle the brand side of this?
evals.expected_output: Should trigger the Reputational Crisis Recovery guidance rather than generic brand advice. Should distinguish this skill's brand-recovery angle from public-relations' crisis-response mechanics (the actual press/statement handling) and product-lifecycle's recall-process mechanics — brand-management's job here is the longer-arc trust-rebuilding work after the immediate crisis is contained. Should ask whether the immediate crisis response (PR, product-lifecycle) is already underway before jumping to brand recovery.
assertions: Triggers Reputational Crisis Recovery guidance specifically
Distinguishes from public-relations' immediate crisis-response mechanics
Distinguishes from product-lifecycle's recall-process mechanics
Asks whether immediate crisis response is already underway

evals.prompt: Our brand guidelines say one thing but half our dealers use their own logos and colors when they advertise us. Is that a big deal?
evals.expected_output: Should identify this as a governance/consistency-enforcement problem across dealer-executed marketing, not just a documentation gap. Should reference brand-guidelines as the standard being violated and note that brand-management's job is enforcing it, not redefining it. Should ask about the distribution model (see marketing-strategy Section 15) since dealer-executed marketing compliance mechanisms differ for owned-stores vs. dealer networks. Should suggest concrete enforcement levers (co-op fund conditions, approved-asset kits) rather than just flagging the problem.
assertions: Identifies this as a governance/enforcement problem, not a documentation gap
References brand-guidelines as the standard and this skill as the enforcement layer
Asks about distribution model / dealer network context
Suggests concrete enforcement mechanisms (e.g., co-op fund conditions)

evals.prompt: We're thinking about extending our brand into a completely new product category. How do we know if that's a good idea or brand dilution?
evals.expected_output: Should treat this as a brand-extension decision requiring a real fit test, not a gut call. Should ask what makes the brand distinctive today (ties to marketing-strategy Section 6, differentiation) and whether the new category can credibly carry that same distinctiveness. Should flag the dilution risk explicitly: extending into an unrelated category can weaken what the core brand stands for even if the new line succeeds commercially. Should reference moat-builder if the extension is being justified by a competitive-advantage argument.
assertions: Treats this as requiring a real fit test, not a gut call
Asks what makes the brand distinctive today, tied to differentiation
Explicitly flags brand dilution risk as a real cost, not just an afterthought
References moat-builder when a competitive-advantage argument is involved
